SUMMARY

American Express Company(AXP-3.79%)reported record quarterly revenue and updated its annual earnings forecast following a divestiture and the implementation of a global restructuring plan. Management stated that the company remains focused on its membership model, prioritizing the acquisition of high-spending, creditworthy customers and expanding its digital payment ecosystem. The company is investing in artificial intelligence to automate transaction processes and personalize customer service while pursuing new partnerships to enhance travel and lifestyle benefits. Strategic initiatives also include the modernization of commercial payment platforms and the expansion of merchant acceptance across international markets.

Full Conference Call Transcript

Operator:Welcome to the American Express Q3 2026 earnings call. At this time, all participants are on a listening mode until we conduct a question and answer session later on. As a reminder, today's call is being recorded. I will now turn the call over to Kartik Ramachandran, Head of Investor Relations.

Kartik Ramachandran:Thank you, Dana, and thank you all for joining today's call. Today's discussion contains forward-looking statements about the company's future business and financial performance. These are based on management's current expectations and are subject to risks and uncertainties. Factors that could cause actual results to differ materially from these statements are included in today's presentation slides and in our reports on file with the SEC. Today's discussion also contains non-GAAP financial measures. Comparable GAAP financial measures are included in this quarter's earnings materials, as well as the prior period earnings materials discussed today. All of these are posted on our website at ir.americanexpress.com.

We will begin today with Steve Squeri, Chairman and CEO, followed by Christophe Le Caillec, Chief Financial Officer. After their remarks, we will move to Q&A. With that, I will turn it over to Steve.

Steve Squeri:Thank you, Kartik. Good morning, and thanks for joining us. We had another strong quarter with record revenues of $20 billion, up 9%, and EPS of $5.42 reported and $4.68 on an adjusted basis. Given our strong performance year to date, we are reaffirming our revenue growth guidance of 10% and raising our EPS guidance to between $18.30 and $18.60 on a reported basis, or between $17.60 and $17.90 on an adjusted basis. There are a number of discrete items in this quarter's results. Christophe will go through them in detail. I will highlight a few of them.

First, with the closing of the Global Business Travel transaction in the quarter, we are dropping two-thirds of the gain to the bottom line. Excluding the impact of the gain, as well as the portion of it we are using for restructuring, adjusted EPS was $4.68. Second, adjusted EPS includes an expense for legal matters, which includes the unreserved portion of the recently announced civil money penalty levied by the OCC. The fine does not impact our full year 2026 guidance. The orders do not impose an asset cap on the company, and the costs associated with the remediation are not anticipated to affect 2027 guidance.

More importantly, the deficiencies cited in the consent order should not have occurred, and we are accountable for addressing them thoroughly. This is critical to our future and to maintaining the trust that our customers, regulators, colleagues, and investors place in us. We have earned that trust over many years, and we can never take it for granted. Also this quarter, as I mentioned, we are using a portion of the gain from the Global Business Travel transaction to continue positioning the company for long-term growth. Our strong business performance throughout the year has enabled us to step up our marketing and technology investments.

We decided to use some of the gain to invest in making the organization more efficient and better prepared for the future. As a result, we took a $336 million charge for restructuring in the quarter, which is expected to result in the elimination of approximately 5% of our positions globally. Because this quarter's charge is somewhat larger than what we typically do, I will take a moment to provide a bit more context. We have got good momentum, but to accelerate innovation and win over the next few years, we needed to become a more agile and efficient organization.

With that objective in mind, earlier this year, I asked the senior leadership team to identify ways to streamline their organizations, align their teams on the most critical deliverables, and reduce layers to speed decision-making. When completed, we believe this exercise will help us operate and execute more effectively and give us greater capacity to invest in our business priorities. I would also like to highlight the latest example of how we are continuing to invest in our membership model to enhance its value to our card members. Yesterday's announcement of our exclusive partnership with Airbnb, which follows the recent announcements of new and expanded Centurion Lounges and our next-generation Corporate Cashback Card and expense management program.

We know that card members enjoy the exceptional variety and scope of Airbnb's network of unique locations, and we are excited to bring over 1 million listings globally into our Amex Travel program, as well as expanding travel benefits for eligible U.S. card members. Next, I would like to talk about how we are thinking about AI and the rise of AI assistance. There has been a lot of talk about how companies are using AI to increase productivity, automate processes, and generally make their organizations more efficient. We are using AI to do all of those things, too.

But I want to talk about AI and agentic commerce from the customer's perspective, how their experience will evolve, and what it means for American Express. It is still early in the game. Agentic transaction volumes are still small, but the direction is clear. AI is fundamentally changing how consumers and businesses discover, compare, decide, pay, and manage their finances and their lives. But while AI agents are able to act on customers' behalf, that does not change who the customer is. Our customer remains the card member, and the job remains the same: deliver differentiated value and have their back. The way I think about AI is simple.

AI gives us the opportunity to make Amex membership even more valuable. We are well-positioned to do just that. Our differentiated assets, closed-loop network, first-party data, and brand built on trust, security, and service are even greater advantages in an AI world. Our goal is to have membership travel with our card members throughout these new AI-powered experiences, shaping recommendations, securing payments, activating the right value, and supporting the customer afterward. In other words, we want to become even more essential to our customers, continuing to embed Amex membership where decisions happen. That's the key idea between the five key areas we're using AI to enhance the customer experience. First, value propositions. Amex membership is all-encompassing.

It's a combination of the unique access, benefits, experiences, rewards, convenience, world-class partnerships, and great service we offer our cardmembers. AI gives us the opportunity to take our value propositions much further. Combining the proprietary insights from our closed loop, our partner relationships, and access to membership experiences to create entirely new forms of value that are more personalized and differentiated than ever before. Take dining. Through Resy and our restaurant partnerships, we are already giving eligible cardmembers access to sought-after restaurants and exclusive experiences. We're now using AI to combine that ecosystem with our understanding of individual cardmembers' tastes and preferences. Our dining companion, for example, uses insights from cardmember spending to make personalized restaurant recommendations.

Looking ahead, we can imagine using AI to better understand the kinds of experiences different cardmembers would enjoy, and then working with our restaurant partners to create distinctive experiences tailored to those interests at a level of personalization and scale we couldn't achieve before. That's the opportunity. Taking something American Express already does exceptionally well and leveraging cutting-edge technology to make it even more personal, relevant, and differentiated. Second, customer acquisition. As AI changes how customers search and choose financial products, our ambition is to help shape the discovery and decision-making process, ensuring that the full value of American Express membership is clear and compelling wherever prospective customers are exploring options.

We're evolving how we reach prospective customers in this new environment, rethinking traditional search and digital channels, optimizing how our products and benefits are discovered and represented by AI platforms, and developing new ways to reach customers through LLMs and agents. At the same time, we're transforming our marketing and acquisition engine. By combining AI and our proprietary data, we can better identify the right prospects, match them with relevant products and offers, and create more personalized shopping, product application, and onboarding experiences. Our goal is to make becoming an American Express member increasingly seamless and tailored to the individual, helping us attract more high-quality customers, improve conversion, and make every marketing dollar work harder. Third, engagement.

AI gives us the opportunity to fundamentally change how cardmembers experience membership, making it more proactive, personalized, and relevant throughout their lives. While we'll do this within our own channels and through partnering with leading AI companies to make our membership assets available through their platforms customers use to discover, plan, and make decisions. Let me give you a few examples. We're deepening our partnership with OpenAI to continue bringing Amex card membership into ChatGPT. Earlier this year, we launched Resy Restaurant Discovery and Reservations in ChatGPT and are working with OpenAI to launch an Amex plugin that will enable cardmembers to discover and enroll in Amex Offers.

We continue to collaborate closely on the future of payments and have built proprietary dining and hotel conversational experiences that use OpenAI models. In our own channels, Wishlist Builder in our travel app uses AI to help customers discover hotels and plan trips. Through our partnership with Perplexity, eligible business card members can now access Amex-curated AI tools for tasks like cash flow forecasting and creating marketing campaigns. Our vision is for Amex membership to become an intelligent, personalized experience, proactively bringing the right experiences and benefits to card members at the right moment wherever their journey begins. Fourth, payments. As AI agents begin to transact on behalf of customers, trust and security become even more important.

Our ambition is to make American Express the trusted way to pay across AI ecosystems, ensuring that card members remain in control and that the protections and differentiated value they expect from us extend into this new way to pay. Right now, we are helping to shape the standards for trusted agentic payments. The principle is straightforward. We need to know who the agent is, what the customer has authorized it to do, and have a secure way to complete the payment. The transaction of the future will carry more than a payment credential. It will carry context.

We outline the capabilities we are building in our Agentic Commerce Experiences, or ACE, developer kit we published in the second quarter, and we are working with several leading AI companies on integrating ACE into their platforms to enable agent-powered transactions. Earlier this month, we also released our Intent Intelligence framework that sets forth a standard to help ensure customer purchase intent is authenticated and preserved. We are developing Agent Purchase Protection to extend the backing of American Express to eligible purchases when registered agents share intent data and then make mistakes. As both a network and an issuer, we are uniquely positioned to connect the card member, the agent, and the merchant throughout the transaction journey.

Our near-term focus is on building these capabilities and integrating with leading partners. But the longer-term opportunity is much bigger, ensuring that whenever and however customers choose to transact, they can do so with confidence, control, and the membership value and backing they expect from American Express. Service has always been a defining part of American Express membership. We intend to combine AI speed, personalization, and proactive capabilities with the empathy, expertise, and judgment of our colleagues so customers get faster, more seamless service when their needs are straightforward, and exceptional personal support when it matters most.

We have been deploying a broad suite of AI tools that help our colleagues access the right information, understand customer needs, develop personalized recommendations, and resolve issues more effectively. We are also expanding the use of AI to strengthen our capabilities in areas like complaints and disputes to identify issues earlier, understand root causes, improve decision-making, and resolve problems faster. We recently launched our first few conversational AI voice agents. Looking ahead, we want to move beyond responding to requests to anticipating and resolving customers' needs end to end. That means delivering even more seamless service across channels, addressing issues before customers need to reach out, and using insights from every interaction to continually improve the customer experience.

Ultimately, we see AI as a powerful accelerator of our long-term growth strategy. It gives us new opportunities to make membership more valuable, attract and engage more customers, drive more of their spend, and serve them more effectively. We're still in the early stages, and we'll continue to invest with discipline, but we believe AI enables us to build on the competitive strengths we've developed over decades and drive sustainable, profitable growth for years to come. To wrap up, the company continues to perform well. We are fortunate to have a premium customer base, which continues to show great strength and stability. We have good momentum, and our financial results continue to be strong.

The progress we're making across the business, together with our talented colleagues who are focused on delivering the best customer experience every day, gives me great confidence in the future. We are on track to deliver another year of 10% revenue growth and mid-teen EPS growth, and more importantly, we have momentum to sustain strong results in the years ahead. I'll now turn it over to Christophe.

Christophe Le Caillec:Thanks, Steve, and good morning, everyone. Q3 was another strong quarter, and we continue to see good momentum across the business. Customer behavior looked very similar to what we've seen over the past year. Strong and consistent spend growth, especially in the T&E categories, balance growth in line with spend, high retention rates, and excellent credit performance. The strength and stability in customer behavior drove revenue up 9% year-over-year, with net card fee growth accelerating to 17%, FX adjusted. This quarter reflected stable VCE engagement, disciplined operating expenses, and continued investment in future growth. We reported GAAP EPS of $5.42 this quarter, up 31%. Before getting into the business trends, let me walk through EPS in more detail.

There are several adjusted and notable items this quarter, and I want to be clear about their impact on our results. First, the sale of our investments in the global business travel group resulted in a gain of $1.11 per share. Second, as we previously said, we expected to use a portion of the gain to support the company's long-term growth, and consistent with that objective, we have taken a restructuring charge of $0.37 per share. Adjusting for the global business travel group gain and the restructuring charge, EPS was $4.68, up 13% year-over-year. Adjusted EPS includes three other notable items this quarter.

First, an increase in legal reserves of $0.51, which includes the remaining portion of the OCC civil money penalty that was not previously reserved for, as well as a reserve for the anticipated settlement of an unrelated matter. The second item is a discrete tax benefit of $0.29 per share. Finally, a $0.24 benefit from the most recent updates to the CECL reserve models. Combined, these three items had no meaningful impact on the adjusted EPS this quarter. Turning to billed business, overall spend was 8% this quarter, in line with the trend of the past four quarters.

This quarter included about a 60 basis point year-over-year impact from the co-brand exits that I previously discussed, with the Amazon co-brand portfolio sale happening midway through the quarter. Sequentially, spend growth also saw a small impact from the last quarter's Amazon Prime Day and other promotional retail days in the U.S. These impacts were mostly concentrated in goods and services, which grew 7% this quarter. Discretionary spending was strong, with T&E up 10% year-over-year. Airline spending accelerated to 13%, while restaurants, our largest T&E category, saw spend growth of 9%. U.S. consumer spending was up 9.4% this quarter, reflecting the continued strength in our premium customer base.

While growth moderated slightly through Q2, it was in line with Q1 and continues to run above the levels we saw in 2024 and 2025. In fact, Q3 is the third highest quarterly growth rate in three years. One year after the U.S. Consumer Platinum refresh, spend retention remains at 99% for the portfolio. Turning to commercial, spend was up 3% this quarter. Excluding the impact of the co-brand portfolio exits, spend growth was 5% for the second consecutive quarter. We are seeing strong take-up on the Graphite Business Cash Unlimited Card that we launched earlier this year.

Looking ahead, our new Corporate Cashback Card and integrated expense management capabilities will give us additional opportunities to drive engagement and spend growth. Spend growth in international was up 11%. Merchant coverage now reaches over 190 million locations globally, up from 160 million a year ago. Outside the U.S., the number of locations accepting Amex has more than doubled over the last four years. We are pleased with the outcomes of our investments in customer acquisition and driving greater engagement from our existing card members. We acquired 3.1 million new cards in the quarter, with 76% of new accounts on fee-paying products. Turning to balances and credit on page 10.

Total balances increased 8% year over year, in line with billed business. Importantly, we continue to grow balances from our premium customer base while maintaining best-in-class credit results. This is very much by design, reflecting our focus on attracting highly creditworthy customers who both spend and borrow with us. The quality of those customers is reflected not only in our credit performance, but also in the economics of our lending business. In fact, this quarter is a good illustration of this dynamic. Balances grew 8%, NII grew at a faster rate at 10%, and write-off dollars only grew at 3%. Delinquency rate remained very low and stable. For the last 15 quarters, the rate has been either 1.2% or 1.3%.

Overall provision expense was $985 million, including a reserve release of $211 million. The reserve release was driven by enhancements to our CECL models. We feel very good about the quality of our credit performance and the stability we see in the portfolio. Turning now to revenue. Revenue was $20.1 billion, up 9% year-over-year. Revenue growth would have been about one percentage point higher, excluding the impact of the small business co-brand portfolio exits. Net interest income was up 10% this quarter, continuing to grow faster than balances. NII growth in the quarter had about a two percentage point impact year over year from the co-brand portfolio exits. Net card fees continue to be our fastest-growing revenue line.

As expected, we have seen an acceleration in growth to 17% FX adjusted this quarter, supported by the very strong results we have seen on the U.S. Platinum refresh. Turning now to expenses. The VCE to revenue ratio was 44.3% this quarter. We are beginning to see growth in card member services moderate following the step-up from the Platinum refresh last year. Looking ahead, we expect VCE growth to moderate significantly in Q4 as we fully lap the Platinum refresh, returning to growth rates more consistent with what we saw before the refresh. We are also continuing to evolve our value propositions in ways that enhance the customer experience and support attractive product economics.

For example, we recently introduced Membership Rewards redemption for statement balances, which has seen strong adoption. This feature provides card members with greater flexibility in how they use their rewards, while also supporting the overall economics of the program. Marketing expense was up 11%, reflecting the additional investments we made in customer acquisition following our strong performance in the first half of the year. On page 18, we can see operating expenses were down 3% year-over-year, reflecting the notable items I mentioned earlier. Excluding the Global Business Travel Group gain, restructuring and legal items, underlying OpEx growth was 3%.

As Steve Squeri said earlier, we have invested significantly in strengthening risk and controls in the past few years, and we will do what's needed to establish a durable and effective program that meets our own and our regulators' expectations. The ongoing investment are in our run rate, and we do not expect the additional cost to impact our 2027 guidance. Before closing, let me address one of the most recurring questions we get about our margins and how they have evolved over the past years, especially as we ramp up marketing and technology spend and invested in richer value propositions via the VCE expenses. The decisions we make are profitability-based and aim at maximizing risk-adjusted returns and capital generation.

Page 19 shows our ROE over the last 16 years. As you can see, we have increased the ROE from an average of 25%-28% ten years ago to around 35% more recently. Over this period of time, we are on track to more than double the size of our revenue and triple EPS. At the same time, we have also reduced the share count by over a quarter. This performance can be tracked back to our spend and fee-based model, characterized by high loyalty and engagement, greater differentiation versus competitors, lower credit risk, including in distress, lower capital intensity, and higher operating leverage from scale. These results in very strong capital generation that we return to shareholders.

In Q3 specifically, we returned $2.2 billion of capital to shareholders, including $1.6 billion of share repurchase and $0.6 billion of dividends. We ended the quarter with a CET1 ratio of 10.9%, reflecting the gain from the sale of GBTG that happened at the end of the quarter. That brings me to guidance. Given our performance year-to-date, we are reaffirming our full-year revenue growth guidance of 10% and raising EPS guidance to a range of $18.30-$18.60 and $17.60-$17.90 on an adjusted basis. With that, I'll turn the call back over to Kartik, and we'll take your questions.

Kartik Ramachandran:Thank you, Christophe. We will now start the Q&A session. We ask that you please limit yourself to just one question. Thank you for your cooperation. Operator?

Operator:Ladies and gentlemen, if you wish to ask a question, please press star then one on your touch tone phone. You will hear a tone indicating that you have been placed in queue. You may remove yourself from the queue at any time by pressing star then two. If you are using a speakerphone, please pick up the handset before pressing the numbers. Our first question is coming from Sanjay Sakhrani of KBW. Please go ahead.

Sanjay Sakhrani:Thank you. Good morning. Steve, definitely appreciated all your comments on the agentic commerce and all the initiatives you guys have. I guess one of the concerns that I have been hearing quite a bit about from investors is just how people might gamify rewards and allocate their spending to the highest rewards benefit. To the extent that would happen, how would you guys adjust your model? Or is there something that you guys can do offensively to stay on the offensive? Thank you.

Steve Squeri:Thanks for the question, Sanjay. I think, look, customers have always had the ability to optimize across cards. Our strategy really has not been to really compete simply on points or rational rewards. I think the other thing that is important to understand is we really do not have a breakage model. So we do not benefit when people do not use our rewards. I think that when you think about the closed loop and the ability to even match our card members' desires and our merchants' desires, I think that gives us a huge advantage. I think our overall model is so much more than just about points.

It is access, it is service, it is security, which I think service and security in AI is going to be even more important. And it is one of the reasons that when I decided what we were going to talk about today, everybody talks about AI from an efficiency perspective and expense reduction productivity, which is very important. But what I wanted to do was to sort of demonstrate across the five key dimensions how it will actually be an accelerator for us.

The last thing I will say is when we have had gamification or when we have had people that do certain things, we have levers within our model, and we have shown this with the Platinum card, where we can get to spend thresholds that require those benefits to be made, which then sort of eliminates that ability to game the system. I think we have a lot of tools at our disposal, but I think the most important tool we have at our disposal is our card members that love our product and love what our product does for them. But again, like anything else, we will see how it all plays out.

Operator:Thank you. The next question is coming from Ryan Nash of Goldman Sachs. Please go ahead.

Ryan Nash:Good morning, everyone.

Steve Squeri:Morning, Ryan.

Christophe Le Caillec:Morning.

Ryan Nash:Morning, Steve. How are you?

Steve Squeri:Great. Thanks.

Ryan Nash:Great to hear. As you think about spend across the company, and Christophe obviously spoke about the strength versus history. Maybe just talk about what you are seeing. Can you maintain this kind of level? Then given Christophe's comments regarding the moderating of VCEs, can you maybe just talk big picture about the potential for mid-teens EPS into next year and your confidence in it? Thank you.

Christophe Le Caillec:Let me start with that. On the VCE, the VCE is performing as we expected, and as you know, this quarter is the quarter we are going to lap the Platinum refresh, which is the event that created this step-up in the VCE ratio. As you think about going forward, and Q4 is going to be a good example for that, you should expect that VCE ratio to stabilize in this kind of range. But the growth rate in terms of the VCE dollars to moderate significantly and either to be more consistent with what we saw pre-refresh. We are not going to get into guidance for 2027 at this stage, Ryan.

You are going to have to wait for January for that. That is going to help us just maintain that mid-teens EPS ambition that we have been using for years to think about the performance of this company. I feel good about that. I will add one more point on the VCE to Steve's comment here. We introduced this quarter amount-based redemption, which is a very convenient way for card members to redeem their points, and we saw a very strong take-up for this. Convenience is also a very important feature here in terms of those VCE and our ability to control that expense. In terms of the spend, listen, we see.

There is a bit of noise this quarter because of the impact coming from the sale of this co-brand portfolio. That creates some discontinuity in the trends. Obviously, we have a lot more information than you have, but when we control for that, we are very pleased with that, with those trends. In this U.S. consumer segment, we are reporting this quarter 9.4% spend growth. It is the third highest we have seen over the last three years, and that is despite the timing of the Amazon Prime Day. It is not only Amazon, as a matter of fact, because large retailers kind of follow the similar schedule.

Despite that headwind that kind of created a lift in Q2 and a bit of a downturn in Q3, we are seeing 9.4% billing growth and very strong growth in discretionary categories such as T&E and airline. A lot of momentum and strength in our billings.

Steve Squeri:The only other thing I would say is that, as Christophe said, airline spending was really high. Restaurant spending continues to be high. It was up 9%. It is the largest T&E category. Just to highlight, Resy restaurants were up 18%. When you go and look at the Fine Hotels + Resorts and The Hotel Collection, that is up 50%. That is just another example of when you marry our card members with our merchants through our programs, how you just get more than 1 + 1 = 2. Those are the kind of things that I think will continue to help drive growth for us as well.

Operator:Thank you. The next question is coming from Don Fandetti of Wells Fargo. Please go ahead.

Don Fandetti:Hi, good morning.

Steve Squeri:Good morning, Don.

Don Fandetti:Thank you. If you look at the banks, they are just continuing to press hard into the premium segment, adding billions to the marketing budgets. I wanted to just get your sense on how you are thinking about market share and U.S. consumer. Then can you comment on the moderation in the international billed business?

Steve Squeri:Yes. Let me go with the second one first. Look, it's 22 straight quarters of double-digit growth rate in international. We went from 13% to 11%. We'll see how that plays out, but 11% growth is still very strong growth. The demographic from a card acquisition perspective, which still continues to be strong, is predominantly millennials and Gen Z. As far as the competitive frame, look, the competitive frame, it really hasn't changed all that much. I think there's a lot more talk about it now, but it's been a battle for 10 years. People continue to step up their game, but we continue to step up our game as well.

Obviously, we've increased our marketing budget over time, but as a result of that, we've also increased our revenue. Let me also be clear about one thing. When we look at the premium segment, we're looking from a revenue perspective. What we're looking for is sort of that three-legged stool, right? Obviously, we drive spend, we drive tremendous card fee income. We're at $3 billion for the quarter, up 17% year-over-year, and we continue down that path. Then obviously, our premium card members want to revolve, and they are revolving, and we're taking advantage of that. Not only are we taking advantage of that, but we take advantage of that with best-in-class credit performance.

I think the challenge or the thing that we continue to face is continue to innovate, and I think we've been doing that. We've been doing that, as you see, across multiple segments, whether it's how we're embedding AI within some of the value propositions, the Airbnb announcement yesterday, which we're very excited about. Then you just look from a corporate and a small business perspective. Yeah, it's competitive and it keeps us on our toes. But we continue to do well. We're getting the share of revenue that we're looking to get, and the results show that.

Operator:Thank you. The next question is coming from Erika Najarian of UBS. Please go ahead.

Erika Najarian:Hi. Thank you so much for taking my question. Hello. Steve Squeri, really appreciate that you sort of addressed the topic at hand upfront. Rewards maxing was not part of my lexicon until recently. I guess I'm wondering, given that you're planning to be at the forefront of AI, does that lead us to conclude that you, unlike some financial institutions that are blocking access from the bots, you will allow AI parties into the system and therefore allow your members to help them maximize their experience? Is there sort of a financial measure that investors can think of when thinking about the future impact, whether it's helping us understand how much of the benefits are already used or optimized?

If AI increases that enjoyment of benefits, does that impact the VCE percentage, but then there's a revenue offset? I guess investors are also thinking about what the financial impact could be of this rewards maxing trend.

Steve Squeri:Yeah. You started out with rewards maxing in the lexicon, and we ended the discussion with rewards maxing. Let me give you my perspective on sort of AI overall. I'll just try and summarize some things that I said. I think when you take a step back, you have to embrace AI, and you have to embrace it, and you have to do what your customers want to do. Having said that, I think in terms of, you've heard a lot about banks that are blocking. Look, we're going to take a risk-based approach, too. We're just not going to let assistants run rogue through our systems. That's not going to happen.

We need to protect our customers, merchants, and we're only going to allow agents access to our systems that are either approved through API or MCP channels. We're also focused on providing a very consistent membership experience, meaning we don't want AI agents to be pinging Resy every four seconds and disadvantaging our other card members. Are we still on? I think so. Okay. Anyway, so we're going to be selectively looking at agents and how they act. Having said that, and as I said within my remarks earlier, I think there's going to be opportunities for us to embed our AI, our own agents within AI platforms. We're doing that today.

What we want to do is make sure that on these AI platforms, our assets are discoverable, much like we're doing with OpenAI, with Resy, and like we'll do with our own things like Wishlist Builder. I think in terms of rewards maximization, we've got a lot of gaming today that goes on, and it's part of the overall mix. But I think with AI, as it might allow people to game a little more, it also will allow us to manage it a little bit better as well by using AI tools to understand what people are doing, and then how do we modify our value proposition. You've seen us do this.

You've seen us do this with a $75,000 limit in terms of passes for the Platinum card, and you'll see other controls that are put into the system. I think it's a little too early in the game to determine what the impact will be on VCE. But what I also would say is, when you look at the entire model, card member engagement is so important to us. And as people continue to engage with our benefits, we tend to get a higher share of wallet. We get better credit benefits out of this and I think ultimately, engagement leads to a better outcome for us.

Operator:Thank you. The next question is coming from Bill Carcache of Piper Sandler. Please go ahead.

Steve Squeri:Hey, Bill.

Bill Carcache:Hey, good morning. You guys have faced many waves of competition for premium card members in the past, but I'd love your thoughts on any changes you might be seeing in the competitive intensity in the current environment. Does it feel any different today, particularly with players like Capital One now operating a closed loop, generating higher returns, and having historically demonstrated a willingness to step up investments to prioritize their long-term positioning, even if that means compromising near-term profitability? I would really love any insights that you can share on what you're watching there. That would be great.

Steve Squeri:Look, I think Citi, Capital One, Chase, everybody is sort of playing in this space. To be honest, we really don't see much different than what we've seen. It's highly competitive. It's been highly competitive, and our assumption is it will remain highly competitive. It's highly competitive because it's a very profitable segment of the card base. We will begin today with Steve Squeri, Chairman and CEO, followed by Christophe Le Caillec, Chief Financial Officer. After their remarks, we will move to Q&A. With that, I will turn it over to Steve.

Steve Squeri:Thank you, Kartik. Good morning, and thanks for joining us. We had another strong quarter with record revenues of $20 billion, up 9%, and EPS of $5.42 reported and $4.68 on an adjusted basis. Given our strong performance year to date, we are reaffirming our revenue growth guidance of 10% and raising our EPS guidance to between $18.30 and $18.60 on a reported basis, or between $17.60 and $17.90 on an adjusted basis. There are a number of discrete items in this quarter's results. Christophe will go through them in detail. I will highlight a few of them.

First, with the closing of the Global Business Travel transaction in the quarter, we are dropping two-thirds of the gain to the bottom line. Excluding the impact of the gain, as well as the portion of it we are using for restructuring, adjusted EPS was $4.68. Second, adjusted EPS includes an expense for legal matters, which includes the unreserved portion of the recently announced civil money penalty levied by the OCC. The fine does not impact our full year 2026 guidance. The orders do not impose an asset cap on the company, and the costs associated with the remediation are not anticipated to affect 2027 guidance.

More importantly, the deficiencies cited in the consent order should not have occurred, and we are accountable for addressing them thoroughly. This is critical to our future and to maintaining the trust that our customers, regulators, colleagues, and investors place in us. We have earned that trust over many years, and we can never take it for granted. Also this quarter, as I mentioned, we are using a portion of the gain from the Global Business Travel transaction to continue positioning the company for long-term growth. Our strong business performance throughout the year has enabled us to step up our marketing and technology investments.

We decided to use some of the gain to invest in making the organization more efficient and better prepared for the future. As a result, we took a $336 million charge for restructuring in the quarter, which is expected to result in the elimination of approximately 5% of our positions globally. Because this quarter's charge is somewhat larger than what we typically do, I will take a moment to provide a bit more context. We have got good momentum, but to accelerate innovation and win over the next few years, we needed to become a more agile and efficient organization.

With that objective in mind, earlier this year, I asked the senior leadership team to identify ways to streamline their organizations, align their teams on the most critical deliverables, and reduce layers to speed decision-making. When completed, we believe this exercise will help us operate and execute more effectively and give us greater capacity to invest in our business priorities. I would also like to highlight the latest example of how we are continuing to invest in our membership model to enhance its value to our card members. Yesterday's announcement of our exclusive partnership with Airbnb, which follows the recent announcements of new and expanded Centurion Lounges and our next-generation Corporate Cashback Card and expense management program.

We know that card members enjoy the exceptional variety and scope of Airbnb's network of unique locations, and we are excited to bring over 1 million listings globally into our Amex Travel program, as well as expanding travel benefits for eligible U.S. card members. Next, I would like to talk about how we are thinking about AI and the rise of AI assistance. There has been a lot of talk about how companies are using AI to increase productivity, automate processes, and generally make their organizations more efficient. We are using AI to do all of those things, too.

But I want to talk about AI and agentic commerce from the customer's perspective, how their experience will evolve, and what it means for American Express. It is still early in the game. Agentic transaction volumes are still small, but the direction is clear. AI is fundamentally changing how consumers and businesses discover, compare, decide, pay, and manage their finances and their lives. But while AI agents are able to act on customers' behalf, that does not change who the customer is. Our customer remains the card member, and the job remains the same: deliver differentiated value and have their back. The way I think about AI is simple.

AI gives us the opportunity to make Amex membership even more valuable. We are well-positioned to do just that. Our differentiated assets, closed-loop network, first-party data, and brand built on trust, security, and service are even greater advantages in an AI world. Our goal is to have membership travel with our card members throughout these new AI-powered experiences, shaping recommendations, securing payments, activating the right value, and supporting the customer afterward. In other words, we want to become even more essential to our customers, continuing to embed Amex membership where decisions happen. That's the key idea between the five key areas we're using AI to enhance the customer experience. First, value propositions. Amex membership is all-encompassing.

It's a combination of the unique access, benefits, experiences, rewards, convenience, world-class partnerships, and great service we offer our cardmembers. AI gives us the opportunity to take our value propositions much further. Combining the proprietary insights from our closed loop, our partner relationships, and access to membership experiences to create entirely new forms of value that are more personalized and differentiated than ever before. Take dining. Through Resy and our restaurant partnerships, we are already giving eligible cardmembers access to sought-after restaurants and exclusive experiences. We're now using AI to combine that ecosystem with our understanding of individual cardmembers' tastes and preferences. Our dining companion, for example, uses insights from cardmember spending to make personalized restaurant recommendations.

Looking ahead, we can imagine using AI to better understand the kinds of experiences different cardmembers would enjoy, and then working with our restaurant partners to create distinctive experiences tailored to those interests at a level of personalization and scale we couldn't achieve before. That's the opportunity. Taking something American Express already does exceptionally well and leveraging cutting-edge technology to make it even more personal, relevant, and differentiated. Second, customer acquisition. As AI changes how customers search and choose financial products, our ambition is to help shape the discovery and decision-making process, ensuring that the full value of American Express membership is clear and compelling wherever prospective customers are exploring options.

We're evolving how we reach prospective customers in this new environment, rethinking traditional search and digital channels, optimizing how our products and benefits are discovered and represented by AI platforms, and developing new ways to reach customers through LLMs and agents. At the same time, we're transforming our marketing and acquisition engine. By combining AI and our proprietary data, we can better identify the right prospects, match them with relevant products and offers, and create more personalized shopping, product application, and onboarding experiences. Our goal is to make becoming an American Express member increasingly seamless and tailored to the individual, helping us attract more high-quality customers, improve conversion, and make every marketing dollar work harder. Third, engagement.

AI gives us the opportunity to fundamentally change how cardmembers experience membership, making it more proactive, personalized, and relevant throughout their lives. While we'll do this within our own channels and through partnering with leading AI companies to make our membership assets available through their platforms customers use to discover, plan, and make decisions. Let me give you a few examples. We're deepening our partnership with OpenAI to continue bringing Amex card membership into ChatGPT. Earlier this year, we launched Resy Restaurant Discovery and Reservations in ChatGPT and are working with OpenAI to launch an Amex plugin that will enable cardmembers to discover and enroll in Amex Offers.

We continue to collaborate closely on the future of payments and have built proprietary dining and hotel conversational experiences that use OpenAI models. In our own channels, Wishlist Builder in our travel app uses AI to help customers discover hotels and plan trips. Through our partnership with Perplexity, eligible business card members can now access Amex-curated AI tools for tasks like cash flow forecasting and creating marketing campaigns. Our vision is for Amex membership to become an intelligent, personalized experience, proactively bringing the right experiences and benefits to card members at the right moment wherever their journey begins. Fourth, payments. As AI agents begin to transact on behalf of customers, trust and security become even more important.

Our ambition is to make American Express the trusted way to pay across AI ecosystems, ensuring that card members remain in control and that the protections and differentiated value they expect from us extend into this new way to pay. Right now, we are helping to shape the standards for trusted agentic payments. The principle is straightforward. We need to know who the agent is, what the customer has authorized it to do, and have a secure way to complete the payment. The transaction of the future will carry more than a payment credential. It will carry context.

We outline the capabilities we are building in our Agentic Commerce Experiences, or ACE, developer kit we published in the second quarter, and we are working with several leading AI companies on integrating ACE into their platforms to enable agent-powered transactions. Earlier this month, we also released our Intent Intelligence framework that sets forth a standard to help ensure customer purchase intent is authenticated and preserved. We are developing Agent Purchase Protection to extend the backing of American Express to eligible purchases when registered agents share intent data and then make mistakes. As both a network and an issuer, we are uniquely positioned to connect the card member, the agent, and the merchant throughout the transaction journey.

Our near-term focus is on building these capabilities and integrating with leading partners. But the longer-term opportunity is much bigger, ensuring that whenever and however customers choose to transact, they can do so with confidence, control, and the membership value and backing they expect from American Express. Service has always been a defining part of American Express membership. We intend to combine AI speed, personalization, and proactive capabilities with the empathy, expertise, and judgment of our colleagues so customers get faster, more seamless service when their needs are straightforward, and exceptional personal support when it matters most.

We have been deploying a broad suite of AI tools that help our colleagues access the right information, understand customer needs, develop personalized recommendations, and resolve issues more effectively. We are also expanding the use of AI to strengthen our capabilities in areas like complaints and disputes to identify issues earlier, understand root causes, improve decision-making, and resolve problems faster. We recently launched our first few conversational AI voice agents. Looking ahead, we want to move beyond responding to requests to anticipating and resolving customers' needs end to end. That means delivering even more seamless service across channels, addressing issues before customers need to reach out, and using insights from every interaction to continually improve the customer experience.

Ultimately, we see AI as a powerful accelerator of our long-term growth strategy. It gives us new opportunities to make membership more valuable, attract and engage more customers, drive more of their spend, and serve them more effectively. We're still in the early stages, and we'll continue to invest with discipline, but we believe AI enables us to build on the competitive strengths we've developed over decades and drive sustainable, profitable growth for years to come. To wrap up, the company continues to perform well. We are fortunate to have a premium customer base, which continues to show great strength and stability. We have good momentum, and our financial results continue to be strong.

The progress we're making across the business, together with our talented colleagues who are focused on delivering the best customer experience every day, gives me great confidence in the future. We are on track to deliver another year of 10% revenue growth and mid-teen EPS growth, and more importantly, we have momentum to sustain strong results in the years ahead.
